# UKIP 2010 Manifesto Summary

## Core Vision: Freedom from the EU

UKIP's 2010 manifesto centres on a fundamental premise: Britain must withdraw from the European Union to reclaim sovereignty, prosperity, and national identity. The party positions itself as the authentic voice of a British majority denied democratic representation by the "LibLabCon-sensus" – the three main parties who allegedly serve EU interests over British citizens.

## The EU Problem

UKIP argues that EU membership costs Britain up to £120 billion annually when including regulatory burdens, with direct contributions of £16.4 billion gross per year. The party dismisses claims that EU membership protects trade and jobs, noting that European companies sell more to Britain than vice versa, making continued trade inevitable post-withdrawal. Over 120,000 EU directives regulate British life without democratic consent, while EU legal mechanisms undermine Britain's constitutional foundations.

## Economic Liberation

Leaving the EU would enable radical economic reform: a flat tax of 31% with an £11,500 threshold, removing millions from income tax; phasing out employers' National Insurance; abolishing inheritance tax; and scrapping costly EU regulations. UKIP proposes reducing the public sector to 1997 levels whilst generating one million skilled manufacturing jobs through defence spending, nuclear power construction, flood defences, and transport infrastructure. Banks would face stricter separation between retail and investment functions under Bank of England oversight.

## Immigration Control

Mass immigration represents a central concern. UKIP proposes an immediate five-year freeze on permanent settlement, followed by an Australian-style points system with an annual cap of 50,000. The party would triple border staff, require visas for all visitors, hold asylum seekers in secure centres, and repeal the Human Rights Act to enable deportations. EU citizens arriving after 2004 would lose preferential treatment.

## Law, Order and Defence

UKIP advocates doubling prison capacity, introducing "three strikes" sentencing, withdrawing from the European Arrest Warrant, and establishing elected Police Boards. Defence spending would increase by 40%, expanding the Army, restoring naval strength, and maintaining nuclear deterrence whilst withdrawing from EU military operations.

## Public Services

Healthcare and education would be democratically reformed through elected County Boards whilst introducing market mechanisms via franchising and voucher systems. The NHS would remain free at point of use but allow opt-outs through health vouchers. Schools would receive vouchers following pupils, enabling parental choice between state, private, and faith schools. Grammar schools would return alongside "professional schools" assessing diverse abilities.

## Pensions and Welfare

Pensioners would receive a simplified, non-means-tested Citizen's Pension of £130 weekly. The complex welfare system would be streamlined into a Basic Cash Benefit, whilst "Workfare" schemes would require benefit recipients to participate in community projects.

## British Identity and Democracy

UKIP promotes "civic nationalism" and "uniculturalism" – a single British culture welcoming all who embrace it. The party would ban the burqa in public buildings, deport radical preachers, create an English Parliament, and introduce binding referendums on major issues. Proportional representation and directly elected local boards would restore democratic accountability.

## Sovereignty Restored

Beyond the EU, Britain would reclaim its World Trade Organisation seat, pursue Commonwealth free trade, and reassert control over fishing grounds devastated by the Common Fisheries Policy. Energy policy would prioritise nuclear power over unreliable renewables, whilst scepticism toward climate change science would guide environmental policy.
